title: Small business SEO services: questions to ask before signing
body_markdown:
Before you sign for small business SEO services, ask what work will happen, who owns your accounts, how enquiries will be measured, and what happens if you leave. A convincing conversation matters, but the proposal should make those answers clear without asking you to become an SEO expert.


**TL;DR**

- Small business SEO services should connect specific work to the customers you want, not just more website traffic.
- Google warns against agencies promising guaranteed first-place rankings.
- Keep ownership of your domain, website and Google accounts; grant your agency appropriate access.
- Request a baseline, a written scope and an explanation of how qualified enquiries will be counted.


## Which questions should you ask before buying small business SEO services?

Start with the questions below. Use the same list for every proposal so you compare the work rather than the confidence of the salesperson. The [SEO services page](https://nsyght.com/services/seo) gives a concrete scope example; compare any proposal against your own situation, not another business's plan.

| Ask the agency | A useful answer includes | A reason to pause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What would you fix first? | Problems on your actual site and why they matter | A package recommended before reviewing your business |
| Which customers are we trying to attract? | Services, locations and suitable enquiries | More traffic, without a definition of a good lead |
| Who owns the accounts and content? | Written ownership and access terms | Accounts registered only to the agency |
| What does the monthly work include? | Deliverables, responsibilities and exclusions | A task list nobody can explain |
| How will we judge progress? | A starting point, completed work and customer actions | Rankings without dates, locations or context |
| What happens if we stop? | Notice requirements and a handover process | Ownership questions postponed until cancellation |

## Why these questions matter

You are not hiring an agency because you need a longer report. You want people who need your service to find you, trust you and get in touch.

Those are different stages. A roofer can attract visitors researching do-it-yourself repairs without receiving suitable replacement enquiries. A dental practice can appear for a treatment it does not offer. More visibility is useful only when it creates an opportunity to serve the right customer.

**Buy a clear explanation of the work, not a promise that search will become predictable.** Google's hiring guidance, updated June 5, 2026, warns that nobody can guarantee a first-place ranking and recommends asking agencies to explain their proposed changes.

## 1. What did you find about my business before recommending this?

Ask the agency to name the services you want to sell, the places you actually serve and the customers you are equipped to help. Then ask what they noticed on your website.

You do not need a full strategy before hiring. You do need evidence that the conversation is about your business, not a sales script with your name inserted.

A useful initial discussion separates problems that prevent people finding you from problems that stop visitors contacting you. An inaccessible service page and a broken enquiry form both deserve attention, but they need different fixes.

Ask for these starting points:

- The service or customer group the agency would prioritize.
- A specific website or business-listing problem it has observed.
- The evidence it would need before choosing the next step.
- Any work that falls outside its ability or the proposed scope.

An honest answer can include uncertainty. Explaining what needs checking is more useful than pretending a brief look proves why your phone is quiet.

## 2. Which searches would bring the right enquiries?

Ask the agency to connect search topics to actual services. A list of popular phrases is not a customer strategy.

For a home-service company, discuss the jobs you accept, the travel distance that makes sense and the work you would rather avoid. For a law firm, discuss practice areas and the jurisdictions you serve. Those boundaries should shape the pages and topics proposed.

Ask how the agency distinguishes people ready to contact a provider from people researching a problem. Both audiences can matter, but a beginner's guide and a service page have different jobs.

Before approving a content plan, check whether your existing website already answers the same question. Publishing another page with slightly different wording is not automatically progress; sometimes improving the existing page is the better use of your budget.

## 3. Who owns my domain, website and Google accounts?

**Ownership should be settled before access is granted.** Ask which accounts remain under your control and which assets are supplied under a separate licence or service agreement.

Your domain is your website address. Your hosting account runs the site. Google Search Console reports how your website appears in Google, while Google Analytics measures recorded website activity. Your Google Business Profile is the business listing customers see in Search and Maps.

Ask for written answers covering:

- Who is the registered owner of the domain and who receives renewal notices.
- Who controls website hosting and administrative access.
- Who owns the Analytics, Search Console and Business Profile accounts.
- What happens to content, photographs, reports and tracking arrangements when work ends.

Do not assume every asset has the same terms. Stock photographs, an agency's software and custom-written copy can have different usage rights. Read the agreement and clarify those differences while everyone is still discussing the engagement calmly.

## 4. What exactly is included each month?

A proposal for small business SEO services should distinguish checking a problem from fixing it. An audit identifies issues; it does not necessarily include the work to resolve them.

Ask whether the agency can edit your website, whether it needs a separate developer and who pays for work outside the agreed scope. Also clarify who approves service descriptions, legal claims, photographs and changes to important pages.

Request a sample plan for the first 30 days and an explanation of the following 60 days. These are planning checkpoints you are requesting, not a promise that rankings or leads will change on a fixed timetable.

For a 2026 proposal, separate these work areas:

- Website access, page checks and technical repairs.
- Improvements to existing service pages and internal links.
- Business Profile management and business-information corrections.
- New content and the research or owner input it requires.
- Reporting, meetings and work that is specifically excluded.

At NSYGHT, the published SEO services scope describes a foundation phase before ongoing growth work. Ask any provider, including NSYGHT, what your starting position changes about that sequence and what would cause the plan to be revised.

## 5. How will you know whether SEO is producing leads?

Ask for a starting record before work begins. It should distinguish Google-search appearances, website visits and enquiries rather than mixing them into a single success claim.

The agency should explain what counts as an enquiry and how it verifies that the measurement works. Someone pressing a phone number is not proof that a conversation happened. A thank-you page view is not, by itself, proof that a valid request reached your inbox.

Request a practical reporting chain:

1. Which relevant searches and pages are becoming visible?
2. Are people visiting the service pages that matter?
3. Are recorded calls or forms reaching your business?
4. Which enquiries turn into suitable appointments, estimates or customers?

The final step needs your input. An agency cannot identify good customers from website visits alone; agree on a simple way to flag spam, wrong-area requests and unsuitable jobs.

For monthly comparisons in 2026, ask for consistent date windows and an explanation of seasonal demand. A report should not call a partial month a decline or credit every enquiry to SEO simply because the website received more traffic.

## 6. What can you promise, and what can you not control?

An agency can commit to agreed work, communication and accountability. It cannot make Google promise a ranking or make every visitor call you.

Ask what progress should look like before sales improve. Useful answers might include repaired pages, verified enquiry measurement and better visibility for a relevant service—not a guarantee that one particular graph will rise every week.

Be cautious when a guarantee relies on unnamed search terms or a narrowly selected location. Ask which searches, which places and which reporting method define success.

**For a 2026 SEO agreement, insist on separate commitments for delivery and outcomes.** The agency should be accountable for doing the work it agreed to do and honest about the results that remain uncertain.

## 7. What does your AI-search work actually involve?

If a proposal adds AI search optimization in 2026, ask for the tasks in ordinary language. New terminology should not make the work harder to inspect.

Ask which customer questions matter, what the agency would improve on your existing pages and how it would check the answers that mention your business. Being mentioned by an assistant, being cited as a source and receiving a visitor are different observations.

A single example of an AI answer is not a reliable trend. Ask how the agency records the question, date and context, and how it will separate visibility from enquiries actually received.

NSYGHT works on SEO and AI-search visibility for local service businesses. The right conversation starts with what customers need to know about your business, not a guarantee that an assistant will recommend you.

## 8. What happens if something goes wrong—or we stop working together?

Ask how changes are approved, how important pages are protected and who responds when the site or enquiry process stops working. You should not need to learn the technical details to know who is responsible.

Then discuss cancellation before signing. Request the notice requirement, any remaining obligations and the steps for transferring access or materials.

Use a short handover checklist:

- Confirm continuing access to your domain, website and Google accounts.
- Obtain an inventory of ongoing tools and services that need replacing.
- Confirm what happens to published content and licensed assets.
- Record who removes agency access after the handover is complete.

An orderly exit is not an accusation. It is a normal part of protecting a business asset.

## Why do small business SEO proposals vary so much?

Different starting points require different work. Compare these scope drivers before deciding which proposal offers better value:

- **Website condition:** repairing inaccessible pages is different from improving a healthy site.
- **Service range:** a single specialist service needs different coverage from several unrelated trades.
- **Geography:** one local service area differs from several genuine business locations.
- **Existing content:** improving useful pages differs from replacing inaccurate or duplicated material.
- **Implementation:** advice-only work differs from research, editing, publishing and verification.

Choose the scope that addresses the problem you can identify. A larger deliverable list is not automatically a better plan, and a smaller one is not automatically inadequate.

## FAQ


**What should small business SEO services include?**

Small business SEO services should define the work, the customer and service targets, account responsibilities, reporting and exclusions. Check whether technical repairs, page improvements, local business-listing work and content are included or quoted separately.

**Can an SEO agency guarantee that my business ranks first?**

No agency can guarantee a first-place Google ranking. Google's hiring guidance warns against those promises; ask for commitments about work, communication and measurement instead.

**Should I keep ownership of my Google Business Profile?**

Keep business control of your Google Business Profile and agree on appropriate agency access. Record who owns the profile and how access is handled when the relationship ends.

**How do I compare SEO proposals without understanding all the terminology?**

Ask each provider to explain the problem, the proposed work and how you will check the result. Compare the written answers using the same questions, and ask for plain-language explanations whenever a term hides the actual task.

**Does a traffic increase prove my SEO is working?**

A traffic increase alone does not prove the work is producing suitable enquiries. Review which services and locations attracted visitors, whether calls or forms reached the business, and which enquiries became customers.

**Should AI-search optimization replace local SEO?**

Do not buy replacement work simply because it carries an AI label. Ask how the proposal supports accurate business information, useful service pages and customer questions, and what additional work is genuinely included.

**What should I ask NSYGHT before getting started?**

Ask NSYGHT which services and locations it would prioritize, what it would address first and how progress would be measured. Confirm the current scope, account ownership, owner responsibilities and cancellation terms in writing.


## One last thing: ask for the explanation, not another report

Before signing, ask the person you will work with to explain one proposed change without using an abbreviation. You should understand what is wrong, what will change and why that matters to your customers.

NSYGHT's small business SEO services are aimed at local-service owners who want stronger search visibility. A useful discovery conversation should leave you clearer about the next decision—even if the decision is to fix an existing problem before buying more content.
